summary: This RFC describes extending a network's broadcast domain over more than one physical network by using a broadcast packet repeater.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 947 describes a broadcast repeater that forwards selected packets between physical networks. A receiving repeater rebroadcasts each packet on its own LAN while retaining the original source address.

what is a broadcast packet repeater

subtitle: A user-level repeater for relaying selected broadcast packets between networks.

tldr.problem: A broadcast packet reaches hosts on its physical network, but not hosts on other networks connected through gateways.
tldr.mechanism: A forwarder selects local broadcast packets and sends them over TCP to repeaters on other networks, where they are rebroadcast locally.
tldr.outcome: The authors report an implementation that extended a broadcast domain across two Ethernets separated by other LANs, with host processing overhead.

today: RFC 947 describes and reports experience with a broadcast repeater implementation for Cronus. It notes the host processing overhead of filtering packets in user-level software.

sections.title: Broadcasts Stop at a Network Boundary
sections.content:
Broadcasting lets a host send one packet to many hosts on its physical network. The memo notes that gateways do not extend those broadcasts across connected LANs, limiting applications that use broadcast to one network.

The authors needed wider broadcast reach for Cronus, which used broadcast to locate resources and collect server status. They say multicast would have been more appropriate but was unavailable in some network implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: A broadcast reaches hosts on its own physical network, not across a gateway. Cronus needed a way to reach selected hosts on distant LANs.

sections.title: Forwarding and Rebroadcasting
sections.content:
A broadcast repeater is a process on a network host that listens for broadcasts and selects which packets to forward. It sends selected packets to repeaters on other LANs using a repeater-to-repeater protocol.

The receiving repeater rebroadcasts the packet on its local LAN and keeps the original source address. The configuration file specifies the repeater addresses and which packets each should receive.
sections.plainLanguage: A forwarder sends selected broadcast packets to remote repeaters. Each remote repeater broadcasts the packet on its own LAN while preserving the source address.

sections.title: Loop Prevention and Experience
sections.content:
The implementation uses separate forwarder and repeater processes. To prevent feedback loops, a forwarder does not connect to a repeater on the same LAN and does not forward packets whose source is not on its own LAN.

The authors report successful operation on a VAX running 4.2 BSD UNIX. They also report overhead because the forwarder wakes for each UDP packet arriving at the host; they discuss kernel filtering or a dedicated microcomputer as alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: The implementation checks packet sources and repeater locations to avoid forwarding loops. The authors report that it worked, but required extra processing on the host.
